stats-hardy-weinberg-s1.title: Flower color in a meadow
stats-hardy-weinberg-s1.text: In a large, randomly mating population of a wildflower, purple (allele A) is completely dominant to white (allele a). A survey of 400 plants found the following. Assume the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for this gene.

stats-hardy-weinberg-s2.title: Genotypes in a small island population
stats-hardy-weinberg-s2.text: Researchers genotyped 100 lizards on a small island for a gene with two alleles, B and b. Critical values of χ²: at p = 0.05, df 1 = 3.84, df 2 = 5.99.

items.q: Calculate q, the frequency of the white allele (a). Give your answer to two decimal places.

why.correct: White plants are aa, so q² = 36 ÷ 400 = 0.09. q = √0.09 = 0.30.

items.q: How many of the 400 plants are expected to be heterozygous (Aa)? Give a whole number.
A student says p = 364 ÷ 400 = 0.91. What is wrong with this?
options: 364 ÷ 400 is the frequency of purple plants, which includes both AA and Aa genotypes, not the frequency of the A allele.
Nothing is wrong: the dominant allele frequency equals the fraction of plants that show the dominant phenotype.
The student should have divided by 800, because each plant carries two copies of the gene for flower color.
The student should have used 36 ÷ 364, comparing white plants with purple plants rather than with the total.

why.correct: Purple plants are AA (p²) plus Aa (2pq): 0.49 + 0.42 = 0.91. The allele frequency p is 0.70. Start from the recessive class, the one phenotype with a single genotype.
options: Correct.
Phenotype frequency (0.91) is not allele frequency (0.70) for a dominant trait.
Counting alleles needs genotype counts; purple plants' genotypes are unknown, so dividing phenotypes by 800 does not work.
A ratio of white to purple is not a frequency of anything in the formula.

items.q: Why must the population be assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for these calculations?
options: Only in equilibrium does the white-flower frequency equal q², so q can be found from it.
Equilibrium guarantees that the population contains exactly 400 plants each generation.
Equilibrium makes the purple allele dominant, which is needed to tell the phenotypes apart.
Equilibrium means the population has no heterozygotes, so the genotypes can be counted.

why.correct: q² = frequency of aa holds when genotypes are in Hardy-Weinberg proportions. If, say, white plants were selected against or mating were not random, q² would not equal the white frequency.
options: Correct.
Equilibrium concerns allele and genotype frequencies, not population size.
Dominance is a property of the alleles, not of equilibrium.
At equilibrium heterozygotes are expected at frequency 2pq.

items.q: Calculate p, the frequency of allele B, from the genotype counts. Give your answer to two decimal places.

why.correct: Count alleles: 100 lizards carry 200 alleles. B alleles = 2 × 50 (BB) + 30 (Bb) = 130. p = 130 ÷ 200 = 0.65.

items.q: How many Bb lizards are expected under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium? Give your answer to one decimal place.
Expected counts are BB 42.25, Bb 45.5, bb 12.25. Calculate χ² to two decimal places.
The chi-square value exceeds the critical value. Which conclusion and explanation fit the data best?
options: Reject Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium: there are fewer heterozygotes than expected, which fits inbreeding in a small island population.
Fail to reject equilibrium: the allele frequencies of 0.65 and 0.35 add up to 1, which shows the population is stable.
Reject equilibrium: there are more heterozygotes than expected, which fits lizards choosing mates unlike themselves.
Reject equilibrium: the population has too few individuals for any Hardy-Weinberg test to be carried out with confidence on an island.

why.correct: Observed Bb (30) is far below expected (45.5), while both homozygotes are above expected. Mating between relatives in a small population raises homozygosity, which matches this pattern.
options: Correct: reject, with a mechanism matched to the pattern.
p + q = 1 by definition in any population; it says nothing about equilibrium.
There are fewer heterozygotes than expected, not more.
A sample of 100 is enough for the test; the problem is the poor fit.

items.q: Teachers disagree whether this test has 1 or 2 degrees of freedom. Why does it not change the decision here?
options: χ² = 11.60 is larger than both 3.84 (df 1) and 5.99 (df 2), so equilibrium is rejected either way.
Degrees of freedom are not used in Hardy-Weinberg tests, which compare genotype counts directly.
With 100 lizards the two critical values are equal, so the choice of df makes no difference.
The decision depends just on whether p + q = 1, which is true with either number of degrees of freedom.

why.correct: Three genotype classes give 3 − 1 = 2 df; estimating p from the same data removes one more, giving 1. Here χ² exceeds both critical values, so the decision is the same.
options: Correct.
Chi-square tests always use df to find the critical value.
Critical values depend on df, not on sample size.
p + q = 1 is always true; the test is about genotype counts.

items.q: A recessive disorder affects 1 in 2,500 newborns in a population assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Calculate the expected frequency of carriers (heterozygotes), to three decimal places.

A recessive disorder affects 1 in 2,500 newborns (q = 0.02), so carriers are about 98 times more common than affected individuals. Which prediction about selection against affected individuals follows?
options: Selection against affected individuals lowers q slowly, because most copies of the recessive allele sit in carriers, who are not selected against.
Selection against affected individuals removes the allele within a generation, because affected people are unable to pass it on to children.
Selection against affected individuals raises q, because carriers then have more offspring than people with two dominant alleles.
Selection has no effect on q, because a recessive allele hidden in heterozygotes is shielded from selection and so stays at the same frequency.

why.correct: With q = 0.02, about 98% of a alleles are in Aa carriers (2pq = 0.0392 holds 0.0196 of the a alleles; aa holds 0.0004). Selection that acts on aa reaches only a tiny share of the alleles, so q falls very slowly.
options: Correct.
Most copies are in carriers, so they persist.
Carriers are not favored in this scenario; selection against aa lowers q, not raises it.
Selection against aa does lower q, just slowly.

items.q: In a beetle population, the recessive green phenotype fell from 25% to 16% over several generations. Calculate the change in q, the green allele frequency (use a minus sign for a decrease), to two decimal places.

why.correct: Before: q = √0.25 = 0.50. After: q = √0.16 = 0.40. Change = 0.40 − 0.50 = −0.10 (assuming each generation was in Hardy-Weinberg proportions when counted).

items.q: In a population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with q = 0.3, which events would be expected to change q in the next generation? Select ALL that apply.
options: Many individuals from a nearby population with q = 0.8 join it
Individuals with the aa genotype survive less often to breed
The population doubles in size by random mating with no selection
Individuals keep choosing mates at random with respect to this gene
Each individual is counted twice in the next survey

why.correct: Gene flow (migrants with a different q) and selection against aa change q. Random mating and growth with no selection keep q constant; counting errors change the estimate, not the population.
options: Changes q: gene flow brings in alleles at a different frequency.
Changes q: selection removes a alleles.
No change: random mating and growth alone do not alter allele frequencies.
No change: random mating is one of the conditions that keeps a population in equilibrium.
No change in the population: this is a measurement mistake.

items.q: If q = 0.4 in a population at equilibrium, what is the frequency of homozygous dominant individuals?

options: Correct.
0.16 is q², the homozygous recessive frequency.
0.48 is 2pq, the heterozygote frequency.
0.60 is p, an allele frequency, not a genotype frequency.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the number of heterozygotes from phenotype counts in order.
options: Divide the number of recessive-phenotype individuals by the total to get q².
Take the square root to get q.
Calculate p = 1 − q.
Calculate 2pq.
Multiply 2pq by the population size.

why.correct: Recessive frequency gives q², then q, then p, then 2pq, then the count.
